{"id": "df9c5352-bcd5-4699-9f71-cd889187dcf8", "role": "assistant", "block_type": "thinking", "content": [{"type": "text", "text": "This is really a general AWS networking question about Direct Connect and Cloud WAN rather than something specific to the agent space resources, so I'm checking whether it falls under the product_knowledge guidance requiring verify_aws_claim for questions about pricing, integrations, security, setup, or how a capability works.

This is a conceptual architecture question about overlapping CIDRs: Direct Connect advertising 10.0.0.0/8 into Cloud WAN while VPCs use 10.1.0.0/16 and 10.2.0.0/16, so I want to verify the exact routing precedence behavior since I have some uncertainty there.

Working through the routing logic, longest-prefix-match within Cloud WAN should still correctly send traffic destined for the VPCs to those VPCs rather than out to Direct Connect, since /16 is more specific than /8. For addresses within 10.0.0.0/8 but outside either /16, the only matching route is the supernet from Direct Connect, so that traffic correctly routes there too -- the real concern must lie elsewhere, maybe in symmetric routing or segment-sharing restrictions.

Longest-prefix match should generally resolve traffic correctly even with overlapping supernets, since Cloud WAN re-advertises the more specific VPC CIDRs back over DX via BGP. But I'm recalling there's a known edge case with Cloud WAN and Transit Gateway where overlapping CIDRs across attachments in the same segment can cause actual problems.

These include asymmetric routing, blackholed traffic if VPC route tables have a static aggregate route pointing elsewhere, and segmentation/isolation breaking down when security boundaries rely on distinct CIDRs. I also recall something about AWS documentation flagging non-overlapping CIDR requirements within segments for Cloud WAN specifically, but my confidence here is moderate at best, so I want to verify this against the actual docs rather than rely on memory.

"}]}

Use this option to\\n control path selection: per-peer longest-prefix routes, active/standby, or\\n ECMP.\\n* **Route installation enabled (default)** \u2013 Cloud WAN\\n installs a system route for each rule's NAT CIDR, with an empty AS path. Traffic\\n to the NAT CIDR is forwarded along the routes your network advertises that\\n overlap the rule's original CIDR. If your network advertises nothing that\\n overlaps the original CIDR, the NAT route drops traffic. Use this option if you\\n can't or prefer not to change your on-premises router configuration.\\n\\nFor these attachment types, the original (pre-NAT) routes your network advertises\\naren't removed in either mode. Translation works the same in both modes. The setting\\ncontrols only route installation\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/network-manager/latest/cloudwan/cloudwan-nat-routing.html\"},{\"rank_order\":3,\"title\":\"How do I configure Direct Connect and VPN failover with Transit Gateway?\",\"context\":\"### (Optional) Prevent asymmetric routing when VPN routes are more specific\\n\\nVPC CIDRs that you advertise from Transit Gateway VPN route tables are more specific than CIDRs that you advertise over a transit virtual interface. {"id": "3fe267f6-3181-48b3-a8a8-8c76b0a7a715", "role": "assistant", "block_type": "tool_summary", "content": [{"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": "tooluse_8qECcgUZ5N02i7SWCjS8c9", "status": "success", "content": [{"text": "{\"content\":{\"result\":[{\"status\":\"SUCCESS\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/network-manager/latest/cloudwan/routing-policies-routeeval.html\",\"content\":\"Note: Page redirected from https://docs.aws.amazon.com/network-manager/latest/cloudwan/routing-policies-routeeval.html to https://docs.aws.amazon.com/network-manager/latest/cloudwan/what-is-cloudwan.html .\\n\\nTable of Contents:\\n- What is AWS Cloud WAN? (char 0-15189)\\n  - Global and core network key concepts (char 2467-10399)\\n  - AWS PrivateLink support (char 10400-11054)\\n  - IPv6 support (char 11055-11257)\\n  - Home Region (char 11258-12873)\\n  - Region availability (char 12874-14822)\\n  - Cloud WAN pricing (char 14823-15189)\\n\\n# What is AWS Cloud WAN?\\n\\nAWS Cloud WAN is a managed wide-area networking (WAN) service that you can use to build, manage,\\nand monitor a unified global network that connects resources running across your cloud and\\non-premises environments. It provides a central dashboard from which you can connect on-premises\\nbranch offices, data centers, and Amazon Virtual Private Clouds (VPCs) across the AWS global\\nnetwork. You can use simple network policies to centrally configure and automate network\\nmanagement and security tasks, and get a complete view of your global network. For key concepts\\nand terms about global and core networks, see Global and core network key concepts.\\n\\n**Note:**\\n\\nAWS Cloud WAN is designed to work with a core network. You can create a core network at the time\\nyou create your global network, or you can create one later on. If you want to create a global\\nnetwork without using a core network, use AWS Global Networks for Transit Gateways. For more\\ninformation, see the *AWS Global\\nNetworks for Transit Gateways User Guide*.\\n\\nThere are a number of ways you can work with AWS Cloud WAN to create and maintain your core network, policies, segments, and attachments:\\n\\n* **AWS Management console**\\n\\n  The AWS Management console provides a web interface for you to create your global and\\n  core networks, policy versions, segments, and attachments. For more information on using the\\n  console to create and maintain your global and core networks, see Quick start: Create a global and core network.\\n* **AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI)**\\n\\n  Provides command-line support for a broad set of AWS services using the command line.\\n  For more information, see the Amazon EC2 command line\\n  reference, which includes AWS Transit Gateway and Amazon VPC, and the AWS Global Networks for Transit Gateways command\\n  line reference.\\n* ****AWS** SDKs**\\n\\n  Provides language-specific API operations and takes care of a number of connection\\n  details, such as calculating signatures, handling request retries, and handling errors. For\\n  more information, see the *AWS Global Networks for Transit Gateways API Reference*.\\n* ****Query API****\\n\\n  Provides low-level API actions using HTTPS requests. Using the Query API is the most direct\\n  way to access Amazon VPC, but it requires that your application handle low-level details\\n  such as generating the hash to sign the request, and handling errors. For more information,\\n  see the *Amazon EC2\\n  API Reference*.\\n\\n## Global and core network key concepts\\n\\nThe following are the key concepts for AWS Cloud WAN:\\n\\n* **Global network**\\n\\n  A single, private network that acts as the high-level container for your\\n  network objects. A global network can contain both AWS Transit Gateways and other AWS Cloud WAN\\n  core networks. These can be seen in the Network Manager console.\\n* **Core network**\\n\\n  The part of your global network managed by AWS. This includes Regional\\n  connection points and attachments, such as VPNs, VPCs, and Transit Gateway\\n  Connects. Your core network operates in the Regions that are defined in your\\n  core network policy document.\\n* **Core network policy**\\n\\n  A core network policy document is a single document applied to your core\\n  network that captures your intent and deploys it for you. The core network\\n  policy is a declarative language that defines segments, AWS Region routing,\\n  and how attachments should map to segments. With a core network policy, you can\\n  describe your intent for access control and traffic routing, and AWS Cloud WAN handles\\n  the configuration details. Some examples of advanced architectures that you can\\n  create with policy include creating a segment for shared services (for example,\\n  service directories or authentication services), providing internet access\\n  through a firewall for a segment, automatically assigning VPCs to segments based\\n  on tags, and defining which AWS Regions a segment is available in.\\n\\n  Over time you might find that you want to make adjustments or additions to\\n  your core network policy. With a policy, you can make any changes or additions\\n  to your core network and apply those changes through an updated JSON policy. You\\n  can do this using either the visual editor on the console, or through an\\n  included JSON editor. You can maintain multiple versions of a policy, although\\n  only one policy can be in effect. At any time, you can update your core network\\n  to use a new policy or revert to a previous version.\\n* **Attachments**\\n\\n  Attachments are any connections or resources that you want to add to your core\\n  network. Supported attachments include VPCs, VPNs, Transit Gateway route table\\n  attachments, and Connect attachments.\\n* **Core network edge**\\n\\n  The Regional connection point managed by AWS in each Region, as defined in the core\\n  network policy. Every attachment connects to a core network edge. This is also known as an\\n  AWS Transit Gateway, and it inherits many of the same properties.\\n\\n  In your core network policy document, you define the AWS Region where you want\\n  connectivity. At any time, you can add or remove AWS Regions using the policy document.\\n  For each AWS Region that you define in the policy document, AWS Cloud WAN then creates a core\\n  network edge router in the specified Region. All core network edges in your core network\\n  create full-mesh peering with each other to form a highly resilient network. Traffic\\n  across the AWS global network uses redundant connections and multiple paths.\\n* **Network segments**\\n\\n  Segments are dedicated routing domains, which means that by default, only\\n  attachments within the same segment can communicate. ## Why this causes problems

**If it's true overlap (on-prem actually uses addresses inside 10.1.0.0/16 or 10.2.0.0/16), not just a broad supernet:**
- Cloud WAN's segment route tables will see the **same specific prefix learned from two attachments** — the VPC attachment and the Direct Connect gateway. When prefixes tie in specificity, Cloud WAN falls back to its documented route-evaluation/tie-break logic (attachment type preference, AS_PATH, etc.) rather than simple longest-prefix-match, so path selection becomes unpredictable and not necessarily what you intended.
- This commonly produces **asymmetric routing** — traffic to the VPC goes one way, return traffic prefers Direct Connect (or vice versa) — which breaks anything stateful in the path (NAT, stateful firewalls, flow-based inspection).
- Worst case: traffic meant for the VPC gets black-holed toward on-premises, or traffic meant for the real on-prem hosts gets delivered into the VPC instead.

**If it's just a coarse /8 advertisement with no actual duplicate addressing underneath:**
- Longest-prefix-match generally protects you — the VPC's more specific /16 routes win for traffic destined to 10.1.0.0/16 and 10.2.0.0/16, so this case is less dangerous.
- But it still over-claims address space in the segment route table: any future VPC or subnet carved out of 10.0.0.0/8 in that segment inherits risk the moment an on-prem block genuinely collides with it, and it weakens the intent of segmentation — a segment meant to scope access narrowly ends up with a Direct Connect attachment that matches nearly the entire private range.

## How to fix it

1. **Eliminate the real overlap first.** If on-prem genuinely has hosts in 10.1.0.0/16 or 10.2.0.0/16, re-IP that block or NAT it — this is the only fix that removes ambiguity outright rather than just managing it.
2. **Use Cloud WAN's native 1:1 NAT for Direct Connect/VPN attachments** if re-IP isn't feasible. Cloud WAN supports NAT translation on DX gateway and Site-to-Site VPN attachments specifically for this overlapping-CIDR scenario — translate the colliding on-prem range before it reaches the segment route table instead of relying on raw routing to sort it out.
3. **Tighten the Direct Connect Gateway's allowed-prefixes list** on the DX gateway association so it only accepts the exact ranges you intend, rather than the full /8. The allowed-prefix list acts as a filter — it won't let you widen beyond what's associated, but you can scope it down to exclude the colliding /16s if the customer's router can be made to advertise more specific, non-overlapping blocks instead of one coarse supernet.
4. **Apply explicit route filters in the Cloud WAN core network policy** on the segment or attachment so the overlapping portions of the DX advertisement are filtered before they're installed in the segment route table.
5. **Have the customer re-advertise more specific, intentional blocks** rather than a blanket /8 — summarizing only the real on-prem ranges in use avoids claiming address space (like 10.1.0.0/16 and 10.2.0.0/16) they don't actually own.
6. **Verify with Cloud WAN's route evaluation/route table output** after any change — confirm the VPC CIDRs remain the more specific, winning routes and that the tie-break logic isn't being invoked unexpectedly (a sign a true duplicate still exists somewhere).
